support.note: Agni = the Asura's embryo, cf. Av. Ātar son of Ahura

words.etymon: pie-lex-h2emsus (packet maps it to pie-root-h2ems-give_birth; the noun is *h₂n̥su-ro-, derivative of *h₂émsus)

cognate: ON áss (gen. pl. ása) < *ansu- ~ Av. ahura- ~ Ved. ásura- (*h₂n̥su-(ro-), cf. Hitt. ḫaššu- 'king'); ON sonr = Ved. sūnú- (*suHnú-), the latter used with ásura- in RV 10.56.6.
drift_or_renewal: Indo-Iranian mostly renews the son-word with *putra- (Av. puθra, Ved. putrā́saḥ); Germanic generalises the possessor to the god-class 'Æsir' (gen. pl.), Indo-Iranian keeps a single Asura (Ahura Mazdā; Dyaus/Varuṇa). The derivational suffix differs (*-u- vs *-u-ro-).
shared_syntax: genitive of *h₂n̥su- 'god-lord' dependent on a noun 'son(s)': ása sonum / ahurahe … puϑra / ásurasya putrā́saḥ.
context: All are divine-genealogical epithets in hymnic/mythological speech: in Avestan the fire is invoked as 'son of Ahura Mazdā' (fixed epithet, 116 CAB units), in the RV the Aṅgirases/Maruts are 'sons of heaven, heroes of the Asura', and Agni is the 'Asura's embryo' (RV 3.29.11); in the Edda the young gods as a group are 'sons of the Æsir' (formulaic, 9 Edda lines, in direct speech at divine assemblies).
note: Weak: 'sons of the god(s)' is a near-universal phrase; what lifts it above chance is only that the possessor is the narrowly distributed *h₂n̥su- lexeme in both traditions. Etymology áss ~ asura is standard handbook knowledge (recalled); the phrase comparison itself is my own.

support.note: Greek lacks the causative but has *supnó- = death by bronze

words.etymon: pie-lex-swopeyeti (packet maps only the root pie-root-swep-sleep)
pie-lex-swepeti (base verb; causative swebban only in support)

cognate: The causative *swop-éye- 'put to sleep': Ved. (ní) svāpáyati = Lat. sōpīre = OE swebban / ON svefja (PGmc *swabjaną).
drift_or_renewal: The causative drifts from 'lull to sleep' to 'kill' in three branches independently attested in the same construction with an instrument of slaying and an enemy as object: Ved. ásvāpayat … háthaiḥ dāsā́nām (Indra 'put to sleep' 30,000 Dāsas with blows), ní dásyum … ásvāpayaḥ; OE sweordum āswefede, sweorde swebban (put to sleep with sword = kill); Lat. leto sopitus. The anchors show the literal sense; the kill-sense, which is the substance of the claim, is in support.
shared_syntax: causative verb + human (enemy) object + instrumental of weapon/blow (Ved. háthaiḥ ~ OE sweord(um) ~ Lat. leto); Vedic with preverb ní (RV 7.55.7d ní jánān svāpayāmasi; 7.19.4 ní dásyum … ásvāpayaḥ).
context: Anchor contexts: RV 7.55 is a charm putting the household to sleep for a night intruder; Beo. 704 the guards sleep as Grendel comes at night; Lucr. 3.431 people lulled in sleep. The support contexts are hero-vs-enemy slaughter narratives (Indra vs Dāsas/Cumuri and Dhuni; Beowulf vs sea-monsters and Grendel), where 'put to sleep with weapon' is a fixed euphemism.
phrase: *(ni) swopéye- h₂éntis/dusmenēs gʷʰn̥-tróbʰis 'put (enemies) to sleep with blows' = slay (pie-lex-swopeyeti)
note: The euphemism 'put to sleep' = 'kill' is natural, so chance is possible; the weight is the same derivative + instrument construction in Vedic and OE. Unrelated mapping issue in this packet: Ved. kṣáya- 'dwelling' (√kṣi 'dwell', *tḱey-) and Lat. situs 'placed' (sinō) are mismapped to *dʰgʷʰey- 'perish', so the φθίω/kṣáya/situs pairing is spurious.

cognate: Ved. vīrá- = Av. vīra- = Umbr. ueiro (*wiHro-); Lat. pecua = Umbr. pequo = Av. pasu- = Ved. paśú- (*peḱu-); Lat. salua seruassis = Umbr. salua seritu (same adjective and verb).
drift_or_renewal: At anchor level the pair is split: the AV anchor keeps *wiHro- (vīreṣu) but itemises *peḱu- into species (aśva, go, aja-avi, as RV 1.114.8 does); Cato keeps *peḱu- (pecua) but renews *wiHro- by pastores ('the men who tend them'), whereas Umbrian keeps ueiro pequo intact. The exact pair is attested in support (Av. pasu vīra, AVP paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ, Umbr. ueiro pequo).
shared_syntax: asyndetic or 'and'-coordinated merism 'men + livestock' as object (or locus) of protection/harm, in a prayer that wards off disease and destruction.
context: Congruent apotropaic prayers: AVŚ 12.2.29 drives away the corpse-eating fire 'that is among our horses, men, cows, goats and sheep'; Cato's lustration prayer to Mars asks him to ward off 'diseases seen and unseen … calamities' and to 'keep shepherds and flocks safe'; Umbrian Iguvine prayer 'keep safe … men, cattle, heads [of grain], fruits'; Av. 'for the protection of cattle and men', RV 1.114.8 'do not harm us in cows, horses; do not slay our men, Rudra'.
phrase: *wiHróm péḱu (*solh₂wó- ser-) 'men and livestock (keep safe)' (pie-lex-wiHros + pie-lex-pekju)
note: Well-known comparison (Watkins: Umbr. ueiro pequo ~ Av. pasu vīra ~ Cato pastores pecuaque, recalled). Confidence is high for the formula; the two anchors carry it only with renewal of one member each, as stated.

cognate: All three branches use a *gʷʰen- nominal: Ved. hantár- (*gʷʰén-tōr), Gk φονεύς/φονεύω (from φόνος *gʷʰón-o-), ON bani / OE bana (*gʷʰon-en-), each with the victim in the genitive.
drift_or_renewal: The suffix is renewed in each branch (-tar- / -εύς / -an-), so only root and construction are shared; in the Germanic anchor (fekk hann bana 'got his death') bani has its secondary sense 'death', while the 'slayer of X' sense is in support (Hrungnis bani, Hundings bani, bonan Ongenþēowes of Hygelac; Sigurðr Fáfnisbani recalled).
shared_syntax: agent noun of *gʷʰen- + objective genitive of the slain adversary, used as an identifying epithet of the hero (Indra hantā́ dásyūnām / asurāṇām; Oedipus who slew the Sphinx; Þórr's hammer Hrungnis bani; Helgi Hundings bani; Hygelac eorla hlēo, bonan Ongenþēowes, Beo. 1968; Sigurðr Fáfnisbani, recalled).
context: Epithets of monster- or enemy-slaying heroes and gods: Indra slayer of Dasyus/Asuras/rivals; Oedipus slayer of the Sphinx (Phoen. 1507; cf. 1760); Eddic heroes named after the adversary they killed. Orestes 'mother's slayer' shows the same construction transferred to kin-murder.
phrase: *gʷʰéntōr + gen. of adversary 'slayer of X' (pie-lex-gwhentoxr; cf. compound *X-gʷʰén-)
note: Part of Watkins' well-known *gʷʰen- 'hero slays adversary' complex (recalled); here the packet really contains the Vedic agent-noun + genitive and the Greek Sphinx-slaying, Germanic only via support.
